title: The emotional arcs of stories are dominated by six basic shapes
authors: Andrew J. Reagan, Lewis Mitchell, Dilan Kiley, Christopher M. Danforth, Peter Sheridan Dodds
key_findings: Sentiment (labMT hedonometer) of 10,000-word sliding windows across 1,327 filtered Project Gutenberg English fiction books.

Three methods (SVD, supervised, unsupervised clustering) converge on six core arcs: Rags to riches (rise), Tragedy/Riches to rags (fall), Man in a hole (fall-rise), Icarus (rise-fall), Cinderella (rise-fall-rise), Oedipus (fall-rise-fall).
Mode 1 (rise/fall) explains 30% of variance; first 12 modes explain 80% (mean-centred).
Hierarchical clustering: Man in a hole ~30%, Tragedy 32%, Oedipus 31%, Rags to riches 5% of corpus.
Highest median downloads: Icarus, Oedipus and two sequential Man-in-a-hole arcs; the most common arcs were not the most popular.
practical_applications: Plan the emotional trajectory of a piece (rise/fall points) separately from its plot events.
Man-in-a-hole (problem then recovery) and double-dip shapes are a defensible default for short problem-solution stories.
limitations: Authors: downloads are 'only a rough proxy for success'.
Measures the emotional valence of the text (syuzhet), not plot; novels 20k-100k words, English, Gutenberg only.
No evidence the arcs transfer to 15-60 s video; extrapolation is CRAFT.
license: CC BY 4.0 (EPJ Data Science open access)

title: The Extended Transportation-Imagery Model: A Meta-Analysis of the Antecedents and Consequences of Consumers' Narrative Transportation
authors: Tom van Laer, Ko de Ruyter, Luca M. Visconti, Martin Wetzels
key_findings: Journal of Consumer Research 40(5):797-817. Read: accepted manuscript (City Research Online eprint 6755) + the authors' 2015 seminar slides (eprint 18870) with the same tables.
Meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes of narrative transportation from 76 published and unpublished articles; inclusion required the Transportation (Green & Brock 2000), Being Hooked or Mysticism scale.
Storyteller antecedents (reliability-adjusted rho): identifiable character .20 (k=16), imaginable plot .29 (k=28), verisimilitude .27 (k=8) - all small.
Receiver antecedents: familiarity .21, attention .29, transportability .30 (medium), education .10, (female) sex .15; age .00 (n.s.; 43% of studies did not report age, 33% had mean age 18-22).

Consequences of transportation: affective response .57 (large), attitude .44, intention .31, belief .26, narrative thought .20, critical thought -.20 (fewer critical thoughts), studies with combined outcomes .36.

Moderator: Transportation scale gives smaller effects (.34) than other scales (.56); the authors attribute the gap to common-method/mood bias and recommend the Transportation scale. File-drawer N 80-6627.
practical_applications: What a storyteller controls (clear character, imaginable plot, plausibility) each has only a small link to transportation; who the audience is (attention, transportability) matters as much.

Once viewers are transported, the link to attitude (.44) and affect (.57) is sizeable - but these are correlations with measured transportation, not the effect of 'using a story' vs not (see BraddockDillard2016, OKeefeHoeken2021).
limitations: Correlational pooled correlations (rho), mostly student samples, Western languages (Dutch, English, French, German, Italian); genre and medium could not be coded as moderators.
license: copyrighted (accepted version in City Research Online)

title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives
authors: Melanie C. Green, Timothy C. Brock
key_findings: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 79(5):701-721.
Transportation = absorption into a story combining attention, imagery and feelings; a Transportation Scale was developed and validated (distinct from need for cognition).

Exp 1 (N=97): more-transported readers of 'Murder at the Mall' held more story-consistent beliefs and rated the sympathetic protagonist more favourably. Exp 2 (N=69): highly transported readers circled fewer 'Pinocchios' (false notes).
Exp 3 (N=274) and Exp 4 (N=258) replicated; in Exp 4 instructions that reduced transportation reduced story-consistent beliefs and evaluations.
Labelling the same story as fact or as fiction generally did not change transportation or the beliefs.
practical_applications: Design for absorption: one concrete scene, sensory detail, no interruptions that break the 'story world'.
A story marked as fiction/dramatisation can still shift beliefs - so health facts inside fictional Mint & Tao stories must be correct.
limitations: Lab text stories, US undergraduates; later studies sometimes found transportation did not mediate persuasion.

title: Stories are to entertain: A structural-affect theory of stories
authors: William F. Brewer, Edward H. Lichtenstein
key_findings: Read: University of Illinois Center for the Study of Reading Technical Report No. 265 (Oct 1982); also published in Journal of Pragmatics 6:473-486.
Stories are the subclass of narratives whose primary discourse force is entertainment.

Surprise: critical information early in the event sequence is omitted from the discourse and revealed late, forcing reinterpretation. Suspense: the initiating event (danger) is given and the outcome delayed. Curiosity: a significant event is omitted but the reader knows it is missing (e.g. a mystery), resolved when enough information is given.

In their experiments, suspense, curiosity and surprise versions produced the predicted affect curves; base narratives without such discourse organisations were not rated as stories by most readers, whereas suspense/surprise/curiosity versions were.
practical_applications: Choose deliberately: suspense (show the danger first), curiosity (show that something happened, withhold what/how), or surprise (hide a key fact, reveal at the end).
limitations: Lab texts, US readers; the report summarises experiments detailed elsewhere (see BrewerLichtenstein1981).
license: copyrighted (tech report digitised, open in IDEALS)

title: Brewer & Lichtenstein (1981) - course summary of 'The Trip Home' experiment
authors: David S. Miall (course page summarising Brewer & Lichtenstein 1981)
key_findings: Six versions of a 4-page story (car bomb). Mean liking (7-pt): Base 2.15, Suspense standard 4.85, Foreshadowing 4.30, Misarranged (outcome first) 3.65, No resolution 3.85, Surprise 4.30.
'Is it a story' rating: No-resolution version fell to 2.75 (vs 5.05 standard) - removing the resolution hurt story-ness most.
A plain event sequence without suspense/surprise structure was rated lowest on both.
practical_applications: Never end a story clip without resolution unless it is an explicit series cliffhanger with a known next episode.
Any affect structure beats a flat chronological list.
limitations: Single story, student sample; page is a secondary course summary; curiosity condition not covered on this page.

title: Memory and comprehension of narrative versus expository texts: A meta-analysis
authors: Raymond A. Mar and colleagues
key_findings: Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 28(3):732-749. 37 articles, 78 samples, 33,078 participants.
Narrative texts better understood and remembered than expository: overall g = .55 [.31, .79]; comprehension g = .48; memory g = .72.
No moderator significant (age, listening vs reading, content control, delay, test format); heterogeneity I2 = 98%; publication bias signal for memory studies.
practical_applications: Wrap educational facts (e.g. eye-health facts) in a short narrative to improve comprehension/recall, but keep the fact itself explicit.
limitations: Only 28% of effects controlled content; few delayed tests (4), few listening studies (8).
Authors caution against forcing all information into narrative form.

title: Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors
authors: Kurt Braddock, James Price Dillard
key_findings: Communication Monographs 83(4):446-467.
Narratives had small positive persuasive effects on beliefs, attitudes, intentions and behaviours (secondary sources report r about .17-.23).
Results suggested unidentified moderators.
practical_applications: Stories persuade a little, not magically; combine story with a clear claim and CTA.
limitations: Full text and abstract not reachable (publisher 403; Semantic Scholar elides the abstract; OpenAlex keyless quota exhausted 2026-11-25).

Search summaries quoting the abstract say fictionality moderator analyses gave MIXED results and that medium and research design did not change effect size; secondary summaries disagree on the direction - do not cite a direction.

title: Impact of narratives on persuasion in health communication: A meta-analysis
authors: Fuyuan Shen, Vivian C. Sheer, Ruobing Li
key_findings: Journal of Advertising 44(2):105-113; 25 studies, N = 9,330.
Overall small effect of narrative on persuasion r = .063.
Audio and video narratives significant; print narratives not significant.
Detection and prevention narratives worked; cessation narratives did not.
practical_applications: Narrative video fits detection/prevention messages (e.g. 'get your eyes checked') better than 'stop doing X' messages.
limitations: O'Keefe & Hoeken (2021) reanalysis found substantial heterogeneity.
Read via abstract-level summaries.

title: Message Design Choices Don't Make Much Difference to Persuasiveness and Can't Be Counted On - Not Even When Moderating Conditions Are Specified
authors: Daniel J. O'Keefe, Hans Hoeken
key_findings: Frontiers in Psychology; reviews 1,149 studies of 30 message-design variations.
Narrative vs non-narrative: mean r = .067 [.028, .105], k = 34, N = 9,330; 95% prediction interval -.107 to .237 (straddles zero).
Median main-effect r across the 30 variations = .10.
Even under specified moderators, prediction intervals included negative effects.
practical_applications: Treat 'story beats facts' as a modest average bet, not a guarantee; test variants with real audiences.
limitations: Only the first ~100k characters of the article were read.

title: Kishotenketsu and its potential applications to prose writing
authors: Gabriel Oh
key_findings: TEXT: Journal of writing and writing courses 29(2), Oct 2025.
Ki (introduction), sho (development), ten (turn/twist), ketsu (conclusion); 'functions by induction' (Fister-Stoga 1993); Hinds (1982) calls it predominant in modern Japanese prose.
Conflict may exist but is not the driving force; allows passive protagonists, cyclical endings, perspective shift at ten.
Kubota (1997): no definitive academic explanation; Chinese/Japanese scholars advise against exact definitions of zhuan/ten; it is a guide, not a rule.
practical_applications: Calm slice-of-life carousels (Mint & Tao) can use ki-sho-ten-ketsu: no villain, the 'ten' slide reframes everything.
limitations: Literary-craft analysis of two novels; no audience data. Origin claims (e.g. Chinese jueju) are disputed in popular sources.

title: Seeing your life story as a Hero's Journey increases meaning in life
authors: Benjamin A. Rogers, Herrison Chicas, John Michael Kelly, Emily Kubin, Michael S. Christian, Frank J. Kachanoff, Jonah Berger, Curtis Puryear, Dan P. McAdams, Kurt Gray
key_findings: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Life stories with more Hero's Journey elements correlated with more meaning in life and flourishing, less depression.
A 're-storying' intervention increased perceived meaning (six studies, >1,700 people per secondary summary).
practical_applications: The Hero's Journey has evidence as a self-narrative frame (meaning-making), which is different from evidence that it makes better ads or clips.
limitations: Does not test audience response to fiction; read via secondary coverage.

title: Folkloristics in the Twenty-First Century (AFS Invited Presidential Plenary Address, 2004)
authors: Alan Dundes
key_findings: Per secondary summaries: Dundes criticised Campbell as a non-expert relying on secondhand material and argued a universal archetype harms folklore study.
Toelken (per same summaries): Campbell selected only stories that fit the pattern.
Campbell's corpus centres on male heroes.
practical_applications: Use the Hero's Journey as an optional writing tool, never as 'the universal structure of all stories'.
limitations: Original address not read; only secondary summaries (Wikipedia, blog).

title: The living handbook of narratology - entries 'Narratology' and 'Narrative Constitution'
authors: Jan Christoph Meister; Michael Scheffel (living handbook of narratology, University of Hamburg)
key_findings: Meister, 'Narratology' (rev. 2014): narratology is a humanities discipline dedicated to the study of the logic, principles and practices of narrative representation.

Scheffel, 'Narrative Constitution' (rev. 2013): fabula/sujet comes from Russian formalism (Shklovsky); Tomashevsky: fabula = 'the totality of motifs in their logical causal-temporal chain', sujet = the same motifs in the sequence in which they are presented; later pairs histoire/discours (Todorov), story/plot (Forster).
practical_applications: Separate WHAT happens (fabula) from HOW/ORDER it is told (syuzhet) when planning a clip - the same events can be told as suspense, curiosity or surprise.
limitations: Read via the handbook's print PDFs (archive site).

title: Meet the creator of the Story Spine, an 8-sentence tool to create and analyze stories (NPR interview)
authors: NPR; Kenn Adams (interviewee)
key_findings: NPR interview (2026): Kenn Adams invented the Story Spine, an eight-sentence exercise: Once upon a time / Every day / But one day / Because of that (x3) / Until finally / Ever since then.
Origin: late 1980s, while with Freestyle Repertory Theatre in New York (short-form improv).
Spread to Pixar via improv teacher Rebecca Stockley, who was hired to teach improvisation to Pixar writers.
practical_applications: Fastest skeleton for 15-60 s stories; 'because of that' forces causality instead of 'and then'.
limitations: Craft tool; no empirical test. The 'rule 4 of Emma Coats's 22 rules' link is not stated in this interview (other secondary sources only).

title: Dan Harmon Story Circle (practitioner explainers)
authors: StudioBinder / Reedsy and others, describing Dan Harmon's method
key_findings: StudioBinder (May 2025): 8 steps - You (comfort zone), Need (want something), Go (unfamiliar situation), Search (adapt), Find (get what they wanted), Take (pay a heavy price), Return (back to familiar situation), Change (having changed).
Presents the Circle as Harmon's later reworking of Campbell's Hero's Journey.
practical_applications: Good for 3-10 min episodes (night-optic, series EPs).
limitations: Craft only; practitioner explainer, not Harmon's own text. The page calls Campbell an 'anthropologist' (he was a literature professor/mythologist) - low editorial rigour.

title: What Makes a Super Bowl Ad Super? Five-Act Dramatic Form Affects Consumer Super Bowl Advertising Ratings
authors: Keith A. Quesenberry, Michael K. Coolsen
key_findings: Journal of Marketing Theory and Practice 22(4):437-454.
Content analysis of 108 Super Bowl commercials over two years coded for Freytag five-act form.
Ads with more acts / full five-act form had higher consumer poll ratings (USA Today Ad Meter).
practical_applications: In 30-60 s ads, a complete mini-story (setup, rise, climax, fall, resolution) is associated with higher likability than a fragment.
limitations: Correlational; Super Bowl ads (US, high budget, ~30-60 s); likability poll, not sales. A press summary called story completeness the sole predictor - stronger than the abstract.

title: Story spoilers don't spoil stories
authors: Jonathan D. Leavitt, Nicholas J. S. Christenfeld
key_findings: Psychological Science; three experiments with short stories of three genres (ironic twist, mystery, literary).
Reported that spoiled stories were enjoyed as much or more than unspoiled ones.
practical_applications: Outcome-first (curiosity) structure can work - but see the failed replications.
limitations: Johnson & Rosenbaum (2015) and Levine, Betzner & Autry (2016) found spoilers reduce enjoyment; result is contested.

title: Spoiler replications: Johnson & Rosenbaum (2015) 'Spoiler Alert' (Communication Research); Levine, Betzner & Autry (2016) (Discourse Processes)
authors: Benjamin K. Johnson, Judith E. Rosenbaum; William H. Levine, Michelle Betzner, Kevin S. Autry
key_findings: Both follow-ups failed to confirm 'spoilers don't spoil' and found spoilers reduced enjoyment.
Levine et al.: a mid-story spoiler had no discernible effect; differences in spoiler format (one sentence vs thematic paragraph) proposed as explanation.
practical_applications: Default: do not give away the payoff of a surprise-structured story in the caption/thumbnail.
limitations: Text stories; read via secondary university news and summaries.

title: Replication of Kidd & Castano (2013) literary-fiction / theory-of-mind effect (3 labs)
authors: Maria Eugenia Panero and colleagues
key_findings: Replication of Kidd & Castano (2013, Science) across 3 labs, N = 792: no RMET advantage for literary fiction after one passage.
Lifetime fiction exposure still predicted RMET.
Kidd & Castano disputed it; van Kuijk et al. reported a replication largely consistent with the original - mixed.
practical_applications: Do not claim 'one story makes people more empathic' in content.
limitations: Read via BPS digest and summaries.

title: Defining identification: A theoretical look at the identification of audiences with media characters
authors: Jonathan Cohen
key_findings: Mass Communication & Society 4(3):245-264.
Identification = experiencing reception and interpretation of the text 'from the inside, as if the events were happening to them'; contrasted with spectatorship (distanced mode).
Distinguishes identification from parasocial interaction, liking/similarity and imitation; identification is internal, imitation is external/behavioural.
Similarity need not be demographic: animated/iconic characters can elicit similarity through shared attributes (e.g. goofy, scared) or similar situations.
practical_applications: Give the viewer a character's goal and point of view in the first beat; faceless characters (Mint & Tao) can still carry identification through clear goals and feelings.
limitations: Theoretical paper - proposes hypotheses, no data.

title: The case of the missing author: just where did the claim that stories are 22 times more memorable than facts alone come from?
authors: Hari Patience-Davies
key_findings: Could not find the '22x more memorable' claim in Bruner's Actual Minds, Possible Worlds; Aaker states it in a video without a method.
Stanford Women's Leadership page still repeats the figure.
practical_applications: Never quote '22 times more memorable'; cite Mar 2021 (g = .55) instead.
limitations: Blog (mirror URL); a myth-tracing exercise, not research.

title: Narrative stories as mediators for serial learning
authors: Gordon H. Bower, Michal C. Clark
key_findings: Psychonomic Science 14(4):181-182. 24 undergraduates; 12 serial lists of 10 concrete nouns; Narrative Ss wove each list into a story (mean 104 s per list), yoked Controls got the same study time.
Immediate recall: median 99.9% (Narrative) vs 99.1% (Control). Final cued recall of all 12 lists: average median 93% vs 13% - six to seven times more, no overlap between groups.
Authors attribute the effect to thematic organisation that reduces interference between lists.
practical_applications: Linking items into a causal mini-story is a memory aid (e.g. a product's 3 features as one scene).
limitations: Small N, stories generated by the learner (not stories told to an audience), serial word lists.
Gamst & Freund (1978, see GamstFreund1978) found no story advantage with one 30-word list and 5 min study - the effect seems to depend on many lists/interference.
Earlier entry carried the wrong DOI (10.3758/BF03329666 = Gamst & Freund 1978); corrected 2026-11-25.

title: Using narratives and storytelling to communicate science with nonexpert audiences
authors: Michael F. Dahlstrom
key_findings: Narratives increase comprehension, interest and engagement for nonexperts (per secondary summaries); can also spread misinformation.
Distinguishes using narrative for comprehension vs persuasion; the ethical question is how, not whether.
practical_applications: Health/optical facts: the story carries attention, the fact must be checked and stated plainly.
limitations: PMC blocked by browser check; read via summaries.

title: Does Oxytocin Increase Trust in Humans? A Critical Review of Research
authors: Gideon Nave, Colin Camerer, Michael McCullough
key_findings: Perspectives on Psychological Science. Evidence does not robustly show human trust is reliably linked to or caused by oxytocin; intranasal OT-trust finding has not replicated well; plasma OT measurement is problematic.
practical_applications: Do not claim 'stories release oxytocin so viewers trust your brand' - neuro-marketing lore.
limitations: About trust experiments, not narrative studies directly; read via abstract summaries.

title: Introduction to Documentary
authors: Bill Nichols
key_findings: Six documentary modes: poetic, expository, observational, participatory, reflexive, performative.
Modes overlap; a mode is a dominant tendency, not a fixed category (per Wikipedia summary quoting Nichols).
practical_applications: Shop/staff mini-docs: observational (watch a fitting), participatory (interview a customer), expository (VO + B-roll explainer).
limitations: Book not read; via encyclopedic/industry summaries (Indiana University Press, 2001; rev. 2010).

title: Emotion-Induced Engagement in Internet Video Advertisements
authors: Thales Teixeira, Michel Wedel, Rik Pieters
key_findings: Journal of Marketing Research 49(2):144-159; facial-expression detection of joy and surprise while viewers watched 30-s ads and could stop (zap).
Joy and surprise affected concentration and retention; effect of joy asymmetric (gains from increases larger than losses from decreases).
practical_applications: Early positive emotion helps keep viewers in short video ads; plan an emotional rise early, not only at the end.
limitations: Lab, 2010-era internet ads; read via abstract/press only.

title: Freytag's Technique of the Drama: An Exposition of Dramatic Composition and Art (trans. Elias J. MacEwan)
authors: Gustav Freytag
key_findings: Authorised translation from the 6th German edition (Scott, Foresman, Chicago 1900); original Die Technik des Dramas (1863).
Source of the 'pyramid' (five parts commonly listed: introduction/exposition, rising action, climax, falling action/return, catastrophe/denouement).
practical_applications: Five-act form for 30-90 s ads (see QuesenberryCoolsen2014).
limitations: Analysis of 19th-c. five-act tragedy; stage names confirmed via secondary sources only - scan not read.

title: Narrative Processing: Building Consumer Connections to Brands
authors: Jennifer Edson Escalas
key_findings: Journal of Consumer Psychology 14(1-2):168-180.

Narratively structured ads elicited more narrative processing than vignette ads; narrative processing related positively to self-brand connections, which related to brand attitudes and intentions (per summaries).
practical_applications: Brand stories should let viewers map the story onto their own life (self-brand connection), not just praise the product.
limitations: Storyboard ads in lab; read via citing papers.

title: Effects of subject-generated stories on recall
authors: Glenn Gamst, Joel S. Freund
key_findings: Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society 12(3):185-188. Two free-recall experiments with a single 30-word list: telling learners to make up a story with the words did not improve mean recall vs standard study instructions, also when study time was varied.
Quotes Bower & Clark (1969) as 93% vs 13% final cued recall and attributes the difference to method (many short lists, interference).
practical_applications: 'Stories help memory' is strongest when many items/lists would otherwise interfere; for one short list of facts the story advantage may vanish.
limitations: Free recall of word lists via the learner's own stories; small student samples.
